source.title: Saddle-To-Saddle Dynamics in Deep ReLU Networks: Low-Rank Bias in the First Saddle Escape
source.authors: Ioannis Bantzis; James B. Simon; Arthur Jacot

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendix, is present. Some equations and figures are flattened in extraction, but the relevant text and figure descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own projected-gradient-descent experiments on a toy ReLU network that test whether increasing width helps find a higher-speed escape direction. Its main theoretical and empirical results concern rank structure, not training classification error on benchmarks.
record.gate_note: The paper does not report training classification error or whether CIFAR-10 training reaches zero error. CIFAR-10 and MNIST results concern singular-value structure; those are not rows for these versions. Its numerical toy experiment tests V2’s width-versus-escape-direction claim, not V2’s teacher-student spurious-local-minimum rate.
record.test_reason: The study measures rank structure and escape directions near the origin. Its width experiment measures success on a norm-constrained localized objective, not convergence to spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student training as V2 specifies. It tests none of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate, but the proven low-rank result concerns optimal escape directions, not every realized first escape. Wider networks more often find a faster non-rank-one direction in the toy experiment; global optimality of the displayed rank-two direction is not proved. Full saddle-to-saddle dynamics with increasing bottleneck rank remain conjectural.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies gradient flow and projected gradient descent on a localized, first-order loss and a toy escape-direction objective; it does not apply the training-error recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Width affects the reported fraction of successful runs in the toy escape-direction experiment; the text does not provide exact per-width rates.

fits_no_version.finding: On the eight-point unit-circle problem, wider depth-three ReLU networks more frequently exceed the best rank-one escape objective under projected gradient descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing width can improve discovery of higher-speed escape directions on a norm-constrained localized loss.

fits_no_version.finding: The best rank-one escape speed is √2−1, while an explicit direction with a rank-two first layer achieves 1/2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal first-saddle escape directions in deep ReLU networks need not have rank-one weights in every layer.

fits_no_version.finding: The theory establishes increasingly strong approximate rank-one structure in deeper layers of optimal escape directions; MNIST and CIFAR-10 experiments illustrate evolving singular-value structure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deep ReLU networks trained from small initialization exhibit a low-rank bias during the first saddle escape, with subsequent rank growth suggested empirically.

record.problems: The width experiment reports successful fractions only in figures, without numerical values, run counts, or uncertainty estimates in the supplied text. The experiments use a toy dataset and projected gradient descent; they do not measure training classification error on CIFAR benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. The MNIST and CIFAR-10 singular-value trajectories do not measure a version's named behavior. Rank-one versus rank-two escape-speed values do not directly measure V2's teacher-student spurious-minimum outcome.

untested.parts: Training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks, including corrupted labels and model-size, stopping-time, or regularization comparisons.
Spurious-local-minimum frequencies in realizable two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, including jointly increasing widths and adding one or two student neurons.
Depth degradation of training error in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks and its prevention by identity shortcuts or the specified initialization recipes.
Activation-matched initialization comparisons measuring training speed or trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian weights.
Loss recovery, sharpness trajectories, or divergence measured relative to learning-rate stability thresholds.
Batch normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including comparisons with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's V2 limits_scope verdict: a different measured outcome is not a scope limitation of V2. The paper's depth comparisons concern plateaus and rank structure, and its initialization analysis does not compare signal-preserving initialization schemes.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and comparisons by model size, stopping time, or regularization.
Teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, standard initialization, and tested teacher/student widths of 6 to 20 neurons.
Plain versus residual shortcuts, depth effects on training error, and the described special initialization or normalization comparisons.
Comparisons of initialization schemes on training speed or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, loss recovery, sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization effects on accuracy speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

rows.subject: depth-3 bias-free ReLU MLP
rows.stage_stated: projected gradient descent on first-order loss objective
rows.operation_detail: Varied network width and measured fraction of runs finding the faster rank-two escape direction.

conditions.value: projected gradient descent with parameter norm constraint ∥θ∥² = 3

rows.measure: Fraction of successful runs, where successful means objective exceeds 2−√2, the best achievable value for rank-one weights.
rows.locator: Figure 2, center and right panels; Section 4.1
rows.note: The paper describes success as finding the faster rank-two escape direction; the width-specific fraction is shown only in the figure and is not numerically stated.
rows.check: The outcome does not measure V2. The success threshold is √2−1 ≈ 0.414, not 2−√2. Figure 2's center panel shows individual width-16 objective trajectories, not a success fraction; any width-16 fraction belongs to the width sweep already recorded in R2.

conditions.value: projected gradient descent with parameter norm constraint ∥θ∥² = 3

rows.measure: Fraction of successful runs, where successful means objective exceeds 2−√2, the best achievable value for rank-one weights.
rows.value: figure only; the text states that as width increases, the fraction of successful runs increases
rows.note: The authors state the trend but do not give numeric fractions or run counts in text. The paper says wider networks are more likely to converge to the faster rank-two escape direction.
rows.check: Increasing success at finding a faster escape direction does not establish reduced spurious-local-minimum rates in V2's teacher-student setting. The success threshold is √2−1 ≈ 0.414, not 2−√2. The qualitative width trend is explicit, but exact fractions and run counts cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The text and Figure 2 report that the fraction of successful runs increases with width, supporting a width effect on finding the faster escape direction, but the study does not measure spurious-minimum rates in teacher-student problems; R1–R2.
